title: Teaching by example
hook: the first teaching is how you live
tomorrow: why did the Buddha almost keep it to himself?

segments.voice: Yesterday, balance: the acrobat and his apprentice, each minding their own footing so both stay up. Mai spent a few slow days getting hers back. Now someone wants her to teach.

Little kids copy everything: the way you fold your hands, the way you sigh at your phone. At the chùa on Sunday, the smallest ones will copy Mai before they understand a word she says. An old story starts the same way, on a city street. A wandering seeker named Sariputta is walking through Rajagaha when he sees a monk on his alms round. The monk isn't preaching. He's just walking: eyes lowered, steps unhurried, robe neat, bowl held quietly. Sariputta can't stop watching. Whoever taught this man to move like that, he thinks, is someone worth finding.
screen: `KIDS COPY EVERYTHING.` → `A STREET IN RAJAGAHA.` → `A MONK, JUST WALKING.` → `WHO TAUGHT HIM THAT?`

segments.voice: The monk is Assaji, one of the Buddha's first companions, and the Vinaya, the monks' book of discipline, tells what happens next. Sariputta waits until the alms round is done, then asks him: who is your teacher, and what does he teach? Assaji's answer is humble. He says he's new to this and can't explain the teaching at length, only its gist. Then he gives one short line about causes: whatever arises from a cause, the Buddha has shown its cause, and how it ends. That's enough. Sariputta's life turns on it. But notice the order. The walk came first. Before a single word, a stranger's way of moving had already said: there's something here worth asking about. That's why Buddhists put sila, conduct, at the base of the path, and why monks train in small things, like how to walk, eat and wear the robe. The training is the teaching, made visible. The Dhammapada says it plainly, in Max Müller's translation: "Let each man direct himself first to what is proper, then let him teach others." For Mai, that's good news. She doesn't need to know everything by Sunday. The kids will learn first from how she sits, how she talks to the shy one, and whether her phone stays in her bag.
screen: `ASSAJI GIVES ONLY THE GIST.` · `THE WALK CAME FIRST.` · `SILA: CONDUCT AT THE BASE.` · `DIRECT YOURSELF FIRST, THEN TEACH.` · then, large: `BY EXAMPLE.`

segments.voice: For the sit, take the posture you'd be glad for a child to copy: feet on the floor, back easy, hands resting, face soft. Nobody's watching, so hold it kindly anyway, the way Assaji walked when he thought no one was looking. When your shoulders creep up, let them settle again.
Teaching by example: the lesson people take from how you live, before you've said a thing. Assaji's walk taught first.
Keep this one: by example, the way Assaji's walk spoke before his words did. See you tomorrow.

screen: `DAY 1751 COUNTS.` → `A LIFE OF PRACTICE · 26 OF 45.` → `TOMORROW: WHY DID THE BUDDHA ALMOST KEEP IT TO HIMSELF?`

howItsDone: Buddhist monks and nuns train in small points of conduct (how to walk, eat and wear the robe) as part of the path; at temple classes, lay teachers often teach children first by how they sit and speak.

Sariputta.meaning: a wandering seeker who became a great disciple of the Buddha

Assaji.meaning: one of the Buddha's first companions, a monk

Rajagaha.meaning: a city in old India where the Buddha often stayed

sila.meaning: conduct, virtue: the base of the Buddhist path

sources.ref: Vinaya Pitaka, Mahavagga I.23 (Sariputta meets Assaji in Rajagaha)

sources.quoted: Let each man direct himself first to what is proper, then let him teach others.

notes: Shape: story. v3 storyline (Mai, days 1751–1764), 'the kids' class': rested after being worn out (1750), Mai is asked by Chị Hạnh to help with the little kids' Sunday class and feels she knows too little (1751); Ava finally asks what she does at the chùa (1752); the class splits over chanting vs breathing games (1753); Mai's own sitting goes dry while Ông waters his bonsai (1754); she doubts it does anything (1755); boredom, and Ava's church's desert monks, the unity beat (1756); a summer bakery job shrinks her practice (1757); finals plus early shifts, no sleep, she tells Mom and sees the doctor (1758); she skipped two Sundays and fibbed about being sick, and goes back to retake the precepts (1759); feeling behind beside Ông's juniper (1760); a sit that feels good, and guilt about enjoying it (1761); Khoa is asked to lead the kids' sit (1762); a kid snores during the sit and Ava's grandmother quotes Proverbs, the second unity beat (1763); packing one bag for the trip with Ông (1764). Days 1742–1750 were not on disk when this was written; the review picks up day 1750 from the index (SN 47.19, balance) and the storyline note in day 1737 (Mai worn out at 1750).

Vinaya Mahavagga I.23 paraphrased: Sariputta sees Assaji on alms round in Rajagaha, impressed by his deportment; Assaji says he is newly ordained and can give only the gist, then speaks the verse on causes ('ye dhamma hetuppabhava…'). The verse is paraphrased, not quoted. Confirm. 'One of the Buddha's first companions': Assaji is among the first five disciples (Mahavagga I.6); count left out on purpose.
Dhammapada 158 quoted from Max Müller 1881; confirm exact wording against the 1881 text.
Monastic training in walking, eating and wearing the robe: the Sekhiya rules of the Patimokkha. Confirm phrasing.
Surprising fact: Sariputta was moved by how Assaji walked before he heard any teaching (Vinaya).
